questions.prompt: When would you use unowned instead of weak, and what happens if you choose wrong?

expectedConcepts.text: unowned is for when the referenced object is guaranteed to outlive the reference
weak is optional and becomes nil when the object deallocates
Accessing an unowned reference after deallocation is a crash
Prefer weak when the lifetime relationship is not guaranteed

misconceptions.text: unowned is just weak without the optional, so it is a convenience choice
unowned has meaningfully better performance so prefer it by default

modelAnswerOutline: Both break strong reference cycles; the difference is what happens at deallocation.
weak is optional and zeroes out — safe, but you handle the nil case.
unowned is non-optional and traps if accessed after the object is gone.
Use unowned only with a real lifetime guarantee, e.g. a child that cannot outlive its parent.
Choosing unowned to dodge optionality without that guarantee is how you ship a crash.

questions.prompt: Does this code leak? Explain precisely why or why not.

expectedConcepts.text: Yes: the closure is stored on self and strongly captures self, forming a cycle
The cycle exists because the closure is stored as a property, not merely passed
Fix with [weak self] and a guard, or by nilling onDone after use

misconceptions.text: any closure that mentions self leaks
adding [weak self] is unnecessary because the closure is called only once

modelAnswerOutline: Yes, it leaks. self holds onDone; onDone captures self strongly.
That is a two-node cycle, so neither is ever released.
The key detail is that the closure is stored — a closure merely passed and executed would not cycle.
Alternative: clear `onDone = nil` once it has run, which breaks the cycle explicitly.
